name: Postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex)
summary: The gyrus behind the central sulcus, receiving the thalamocortical projections from the ventral posterior nuclei and mapping the contralateral body in a sensory homunculus that mirrors the motor one: leg and foot on the medial paracentral lobule, hand at the convexity with a large representation, face and tongue lowest. Area 3b in the posterior wall of the central sulcus receives cutaneous touch, area 3a proprioception, and areas 1 and 2 elaborate texture and shape. Its lesions abolish the discriminative aspects of sensation while crude pain and touch survive in the thalamus.

anatomy.location: Between the central sulcus in front and the postcentral sulcus behind, from the lateral sulcus over the vertex to the posterior paracentral lobule on the medial surface; thinner cortex than the precentral gyrus.

afferents.via: posterior limb of the internal capsule

function: Conscious discriminative touch, proprioception, vibration and localization of pain and temperature for the contralateral body; first stage of tactile object recognition.

bestView.label: postcentral gyrus behind the hand knob
postcentral gyrus behind the central sulcus

imaging.normalAppearance: The gyrus behind the central sulcus, thinner than the precentral gyrus on T1; the hand area faces the motor hand knob across the sulcus. Cortical infarcts here are thin ribbons on DWI.

pathology.finding: Ribbon of restricted diffusion along the postcentral gyrus, giving a cortical sensory syndrome sometimes misread as a peripheral lesion.
Focal cortical lesion with tingling marching along the homunculus.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; FLAIR and EEG for seizures

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of two-point discrimination, graphesthesia, stereognosis and localization on the opposite side
Sensory extinction to double simultaneous stimulation
Pseudoathetosis and clumsiness of the hand

examination: Two-point discrimination, graphesthesia, stereognosis, joint position sense
pearls: Cortical sensory loss makes a hand useless despite normal strength: the 'useless hand' of a parietal stroke
Sensory marching seizures (Jacksonian sensory) start at the hand or face, the largest representations
